lessonTitle: Air-Fuel Ratio, Volumetric Efficiency and Emissions

blocks.text: A spark-ignition engine on a motorway burns fuel and air in a ratio held within about two per cent of 14.7 to 1 by mass, because the catalytic converter in its exhaust only cleans up three pollutants at once in that narrow band. Move the mixture a little lean and nitrogen oxides climb; move it rich and carbon monoxide soars. How much air the engine actually breathes, how its mixture is set, and how hard it is compressed together decide both its output and its emissions.

blocks.markdown: An engine produces power in proportion to the mass of air it inhales, since the fuel that can be burned is tied to the air by the mixture ratio. The measure of how well an engine fills its cylinders is the **volumetric efficiency**. The **air-fuel ratio** and **equivalence ratio** describe the mixture, which affects the combustion temperature and therefore the emissions. Finally, the **compression ratio** controls the ideal thermal efficiency but also the risk of knock.

blocks.title: Volumetric efficiency
blocks.text: For a four-stroke engine the **volumetric efficiency** is the actual mass flow of air drawn in divided by the mass flow that would fill the swept volume at the intake air density $\rho_i$: $\eta_v=\dot m_a/(\rho_i V_dN/120)$, where $V_d$ is total displacement (m$^3$) and $N$ speed (rpm); the factor 120 arises because the cylinder fills once every two revolutions. The intake density is $\rho_i=p_i/(RT_i)$ with $R=0.287$ kJ/(kg K) for air.

blocks.caption: Volumetric efficiency of a four-stroke engine (total displacement V_d, speed N in rpm)

blocks.title: Volumetric efficiency from a measured air flow
blocks.prompt: A 2 L four-stroke engine runs at 4000 rpm. Intake air is at 101.325 kPa and 293 K, and the measured air mass flow is 0.069 kg/s. Find the volumetric efficiency.

steps.text: Intake density from the ideal gas law.
Swept volume flow rate: one fill per two revolutions.

blocks.answer: The volumetric efficiency is about 0.859, which is typical of a naturally aspirated engine at this speed (typical range 0.75 to 0.90).

blocks.title: Air-fuel ratio and equivalence ratio
blocks.text: The **air-fuel ratio** $AF=\dot m_a/\dot m_f$ is the mass of air per unit mass of fuel; for gasoline the **stoichiometric** value, with just enough air for complete combustion, is about 14.7 (typical). The **equivalence ratio** is $\phi=(F/A)/(F/A)_{st}=AF_{st}/AF$. A mixture with $\phi<1$ is **lean** (excess air), $\phi=1$ is stoichiometric and $\phi>1$ is **rich** (excess fuel).

blocks.title: Mixture and fuel flow
blocks.prompt: For the engine above, the air-fuel ratio is 16.5 with stoichiometric ratio 14.7. Find the equivalence ratio and fuel flow.

steps.text: Fuel mass flow from the air flow and air-fuel ratio.

blocks.answer: The mixture is lean, with $\phi\approx0.891$, and the fuel flow is about 0.00418 kg/s (4.18 g/s).

rows: Highest: hot flame with excess oxygen
blocks.caption: Typical trend of spark-ignition engine emissions with equivalence ratio

blocks.markdown: **Compression ratio, efficiency and knock.** The ideal air-standard Otto cycle has a thermal efficiency that depends only on the compression ratio $r=V_{max}/V_{min}$ and the ratio of specific heats $k$. Raising $r$ lifts the efficiency, but it also raises the pressure and temperature of the unburned end gas before the flame reaches it. If the end gas autoignites, **knock** results: a sharp pressure oscillation that can damage the piston. Fuels of higher octane number resist autoignition, so they permit a higher compression ratio.

blocks.title: Gain from a higher compression ratio
blocks.prompt: Compare the ideal Otto efficiency of an engine with compression ratios 8, 10 and 12 ($k=1.4$).
blocks.answer: The efficiency rises from 0.565 to 0.602 to 0.63. Each additional step brings a smaller gain, while the knock risk keeps increasing, so the compression ratio of a petrol engine is limited by fuel octane.

items: Use the intake density, not standard density, when computing volumetric efficiency; boosted or hot-intake engines differ.
Convert fuel and air flows to an air-fuel ratio, then to $\phi$, and use the table to predict the emission trends.
Remember that ideal Otto efficiency is an upper bound; real brake thermal efficiency is much lower because of heat loss, finite burn time and friction.
Discuss any increase in compression ratio together with the fuel octane rating and knock margin.

blocks.title: Trade-offs in mixture setting
blocks.text: Slightly lean mixtures give the best fuel economy and low CO, but the highest NO$_x$. Rich mixtures give maximum power and cool the combustion, but waste fuel and produce CO and hydrocarbons. A three-way catalyst needs $\phi$ close to 1, so spark-ignition engines usually run at stoichiometric with closed-loop oxygen-sensor control.

points: Volumetric efficiency $\eta_v=\dot m_a/(\rho_iV_dN/120)$ measures the cylinder filling of a four-stroke engine.
Equivalence ratio $\phi=AF_{st}/AF$: rich gives CO and HC, slightly lean gives the most NO$_x$, and a three-way catalyst needs $\phi\approx1$.
Ideal Otto efficiency $1-r^{1-k}$ rises with compression ratio, but knock limits the ratio for a given fuel.

questions.stem: Volumetric efficiency of a four-stroke engine is best defined as:

options.text: the actual air mass drawn in per cycle divided by the mass that would fill the displacement at the intake density
the brake power divided by the indicated power
the fuel energy divided by the air energy
the ratio of exhaust gas volume to intake volume

questions.correctOptionText: the actual air mass drawn in per cycle divided by the mass that would fill the displacement at the intake density

distractorRationale.a: Correct: actual air mass over the full-cylinder mass at intake density.
distractorRationale.b: This is the mechanical efficiency, not the volumetric efficiency.
distractorRationale.c: There is no such measure of air energy; volumetric efficiency compares air mass flows.
distractorRationale.d: The comparison is of the actual air mass flow with the ideal full-cylinder mass flow.

questions.explanation: Volumetric efficiency measures how completely the cylinders fill with fresh air. It is $\dot m_a$ divided by $\rho_i\dot V_d$, where $\dot V_d=V_dN/120$ is the swept volume flow rate of a four-stroke engine.

questions.stem: A spark-ignition engine runs with an equivalence ratio of 1.15. Which pollutant is expected to be very high?

options.text: Nitrogen oxides, because the flame is hottest in rich mixtures
Carbon monoxide, because there is not enough oxygen to burn all the carbon to CO$_2$
Carbon dioxide, which is the only product of complete combustion in excess fuel
No significant pollutant, because rich mixtures burn cleanly

questions.correctOptionText: Carbon monoxide, because there is not enough oxygen to burn all the carbon to CO$_2$

distractorRationale.a: NO$_x$ is low in rich mixtures: there is little free oxygen and the flame is cooler than at slightly lean mixtures.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: rich mixtures lack oxygen, giving carbon monoxide.
distractorRationale.c: With excess fuel, combustion is incomplete, so CO and unburned hydrocarbons replace some of the CO$_2$.
distractorRationale.d: Rich mixtures produce the highest CO and hydrocarbon emissions.

questions.explanation: An equivalence ratio above 1 is rich: fuel is in excess, so there is too little oxygen to complete oxidation and carbon monoxide and unburned hydrocarbons form. NO$_x$ is low because oxygen is scarce and the flame is cooler.

questions.stem: A 1.6 L four-stroke engine runs at 3000 rpm with intake air density 1.20 kg/m$^3$ and a measured air flow of 0.0408 kg/s. Its volumetric efficiency is:

distractorRationale.a: Uses one cycle per revolution, which is correct for a two-stroke but not a four-stroke engine.
distractorRationale.b: Inverts the ratio, giving a value above one.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: measured flow over the ideal full-cylinder flow.
distractorRationale.d: Omits the intake density; the quantity obtained is a density, not an efficiency.

questions.explanation: The ideal air flow is $1.20\times0.0016\times3000/120=0.048$ kg/s. The measured flow of 0.0408 kg/s gives $\eta_v=0.0408/0.048=0.85$.

questions.stem: At which mixture does a spark-ignition engine emit the most nitrogen oxides?

options.text: Very rich, because the flame is hottest with excess fuel
Very lean, because there is the most oxygen
At idle with a closed throttle, regardless of mixture
Slightly lean of stoichiometric, because the flame is hot and oxygen is available

questions.correctOptionText: Slightly lean of stoichiometric, because the flame is hot and oxygen is available

distractorRationale.a: Rich flames have too little oxygen and are cooler, so NO$_x$ is low.
distractorRationale.b: Very lean flames are cool, so the NO$_x$ formation rate falls.
distractorRationale.c: The mixture and temperature, not the throttle position alone, determine NO$_x$.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: hot flame with oxygen available.

questions.explanation: NO$_x$ formation needs both high temperature (to break the N$_2$ bond) and free oxygen. Both are present slightly lean of stoichiometric ($\phi\approx0.9$ to 0.95). Rich mixtures lack oxygen and very lean mixtures burn cooler.

questions.stem: A designer raises the compression ratio of a petrol engine from 8 to 10 using the same fuel. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The ideal Otto efficiency rises from about 0.565 to about 0.602, but the knock risk also increases
The ideal Otto efficiency falls, because the heat rejected rises
The ideal Otto efficiency is unchanged, because it depends only on the fuel
The knock risk decreases, because the mixture burns faster

questions.correctOptionText: The ideal Otto efficiency rises from about 0.565 to about 0.602, but the knock risk also increases

distractorRationale.a: Correct: efficiency rises while the knock risk rises.
distractorRationale.c: It depends on the compression ratio and $k$.
distractorRationale.d: Higher compression raises the end-gas temperature and pressure, increasing the tendency to autoignite.

questions.explanation: $\eta=1-8^{-0.4}=0.565$ and $1-10^{-0.4}=0.602$, so efficiency improves. But the compressed end gas is hotter and at higher pressure, so it is more likely to autoignite, which is knock.

questions.stem: A 2.5 L four-stroke engine runs at 5000 rpm drawing air at 101.325 kPa and 298 K ($R=0.287$ kJ/(kg K)). The measured air mass flow is 0.1050 kg/s. Find the volumetric efficiency as a fraction.
questions.explanation: The intake density is $101.325/(0.287\times298)=1.185$ kg/m$^3$. The swept volume flow is $0.0025\times5000/120=0.1042$ m$^3$/s, so the ideal flow is 0.1234 kg/s. The efficiency is $0.1050/0.1234=0.851$.

questions.stem: Find the ideal air-standard Otto cycle efficiency (as a fraction) for a compression ratio of 11 with $k=1.4$.
questions.explanation: $\eta=1-r^{1-k}=1-11^{-0.4}=1-0.3832=0.6168$. A real engine, with heat loss, finite combustion time and friction, achieves a brake efficiency well below this.

questions.stem: An engine takes in air at 0.0500 kg/s and burns fuel at 0.00350 kg/s. The stoichiometric air-fuel ratio of the fuel is 14.7. Find the equivalence ratio.
questions.explanation: The air-fuel ratio is $0.0500/0.00350=14.29$. The equivalence ratio is $\phi=14.7/14.29=1.03$, so the mixture is slightly rich and CO and HC emissions will be above their stoichiometric values.

questions.stem: Explain how the equivalence ratio affects the emissions of carbon monoxide, hydrocarbons and nitrogen oxides in a spark-ignition engine, why most such engines run at stoichiometric mixture, and how raising the compression ratio would change the emissions and the knock margin.
markingGuide: Rich (phi > 1): lack of oxygen gives high CO and HC; NOx low because flame cooler and little oxygen
Slightly lean (phi about 0.9 to 0.95): lowest CO, high NOx because high temperature plus oxygen
Very lean: NOx falls (cool flame) but HC rises due to misfire or partial burn
Stoichiometric: a three-way catalyst can simultaneously oxidise CO and HC and reduce NOx when phi is within a narrow band, so closed-loop control holds phi near 1
Higher compression ratio raises combustion temperature and end-gas pressure, which tends to raise NOx and reduces knock margin
Higher octane fuel or retarded ignition or lower intake temperature can restore margin
questions.explanation: Mixture strength sets the competition between oxygen availability and flame temperature: NO$_x$ peaks slightly lean, CO and HC rise as the mixture becomes rich. Stoichiometric operation allows the three-way catalyst to clean all three, so it is normally used. A higher compression ratio raises temperatures and pressures, increasing NO$_x$ and the likelihood of knock.

questions.stem: Derive the ideal Otto cycle efficiency from the heat added and rejected at constant volume, state why a real engine's efficiency is lower, and explain what limits the compression ratio of a spark-ignition engine.
markingGuide: Otto cycle: isentropic compression, constant-volume heat addition, isentropic expansion, constant-volume heat rejection
Heat added q_in = c_v (T3 - T2); heat rejected q_out = c_v (T4 - T1)
Isentropic relations T2/T1 = T3/T4 = r^(k-1), so T4/T1 = T3/T2 and eta = 1 - T1/T2
Real engine lower: heat loss to walls, finite burn time, incomplete combustion, variable specific heats, friction and pumping
Compression ratio limited by knock (autoignition of end gas), so by fuel octane; also by NOx and structural limits
questions.explanation: The efficiency is $1-q_{out}/q_{in}$. With isentropic compression and expansion between the same volumes, the temperature ratios are equal, so $\eta=1-T_1/T_2=1-r^{1-k}$. Practical engines are limited by knock rather than by thermodynamics.
